title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology (9700)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology 9700 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027 (version 1, published September 2022)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and sub-topic headings (1 Cell structure ... 19.3 Genetically modified organisms in agriculture) are transcribed with their printed numbers; objective codes are the printed learning-outcome references (topic, sub-topic, outcome number, e.g. 11.1.2, as the syllabus cross-refers). Objectives paraphrase the learning outcomes in our own words. The three sections and the practical-skills topics P3 and P5 (with codes P3.1 ... P5.2.3) are ours, summarising the Practical assessment section and the Mathematical requirements. No syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-09): the official PDF 'Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology 9700 syllabus for 2025, 2026 and 2027', version 1, published September 2022, read through a pdftotext rendering. Exams in the June and November series (March for India). Check the headings and objective codes against the PDF.

Routes as printed: AS Level only (Papers 1, 2 and 3 in one series; grades a-e); A Level staged over two years (AS in year 1, carried forward, then Papers 4 and 5); A Level in one series (all five papers; grades A*-E). Route A here covers both A Level routes.

Weightings: Paper 1 31% of AS and 15.5% of A Level; Paper 2 46% and 23%; Paper 3 23% and 11.5%; Paper 4 38.5% of A Level; Paper 5 11.5% of A Level. weightingPercent records the A Level share; the AS shares are in each paper's description.

Topics 1-11 are AS content (Papers 1 and 2, assumed knowledge for Paper 4); topics 12-19 are A Level only (Paper 4). Meiosis and genetic crosses (16), respiration (12) and photosynthesis (13) are therefore A Level only for Cambridge although ZIMSEC teaches them in Form 5. The statistics (chi-squared, t-test, standard deviation, standard error, 95% confidence intervals, Hardy-Weinberg, Lincoln index, Simpson's index, Pearson and Spearman correlation) are A Level only; formulae and critical-value tables are provided in the examination, and degrees of freedom must be known.

Papers 3 and 5 test practical skills (AO3) in contexts that may lie outside the syllabus content. Paper 3 (40 marks) gives about 15-17 marks to manipulation, measurement and observation, 11-13 to presentation and 11-13 to analysis, conclusions and evaluation; Paper 5 (30 marks) about 14-16 to planning and 14-16 to analysis, conclusions and evaluation. The practical paper cannot be simulated; written items practise its skills.
Paper 2 and Paper 4 question structures and part marks are not printed in the syllabus; our practice exam-format items use a convention that a reviewer must check against recent papers.
This syllabus is for examination in 2025-2027. Candidates from 2028 will follow a later syllabus (not in the repository); check the Cambridge website for it and add a new version file.
overview: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology (9700) is a two-stage course. The AS Level content (topics 1-11) covers cell structure and microscopy, biological molecules, enzymes, cell membranes and transport, the mitotic cell cycle, nucleic acids and protein synthesis, transport in plants and mammals, gas exchange, infectious diseases and immunity. The A Level content (topics 12-19) adds energy and respiration, photosynthesis, homeostasis, control and coordination, inheritance, selection and evolution, classification, biodiversity and conservation, and genetic technology, with statistical analysis of biological data and higher-level practical skills.
assessmentOverview: AS Level candidates take Paper 1 Multiple Choice (1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks), Paper 2 AS Level Structured Questions (1 hour 15 minutes, 60 marks) and Paper 3 Advanced Practical Skills (2 hours, 40 marks). A Level candidates also take Paper 4 A Level Structured Questions (2 hours, 100 marks) and Paper 5 Planning, Analysis and Evaluation (1 hour 15 minutes, 30 marks), either in the same series or a later one, carrying forward their AS result.

components.name: Paper 1: Multiple Choice
components.description: 40 four-option multiple-choice questions on the AS Level content (AO1 and AO2). 31% of AS Level, 15.5% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 2: AS Level Structured Questions
components.description: Structured questions on the AS Level content (AO1 and AO2). 46% of AS Level, 23% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 3: Advanced Practical Skills
components.description: A laboratory practical test of two or three questions (AO3): an investigation and light-microscope work, in contexts from AS Level biology. 23% of AS Level, 11.5% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 4: A Level Structured Questions
components.description: Structured questions on the A Level content, with AS Level content assumed (AO1 and AO2). 38.5% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 5: Planning, Analysis and Evaluation
components.description: A written paper of two or more questions on planning investigations and analysing and evaluating given data, including statistics (AO3); no laboratory work. 11.5% of A Level.

routes.name: AS Level
routes.description: Papers 1, 2 and 3 (grades a-e). Also the first year of the staged A Level route.

routes.name: A Level
routes.description: All five papers, in one series or staged (AS Level carried forward, then Papers 4 and 5) (grades A*-E).

topics.name: AS Level subject content
topics.description: Topics 1-11: studied by all candidates; examined in Papers 1 and 2 and assumed knowledge for Paper 4.

objectives.text: Make temporary preparations of cellular material for viewing with a light microscope.
Draw cells from microscope slides and photomicrographs.
Calculate magnifications of images and actual sizes of specimens from drawings, photomicrographs and electron micrographs (scanning and transmission).
Use an eyepiece graticule and stage micrometer to measure, in mm, µm and nm.
Define resolution and magnification and explain how they differ in light and electron microscopy.

children.name: Cells as the basic units of living organisms
children.description: Temporary preparations and drawing (1.1.1-1.1.2) are taught with the plant and animal cell lesson covered here.

objectives.text: Recognise the organelles of eukaryotic cells (membranes, nucleus, ER, Golgi body, mitochondria, ribosomes, lysosomes, centrioles, cilia, microvilli, chloroplasts, cell wall, plasmodesmata, vacuole and tonoplast) and outline their structures and functions.
Describe and interpret photomicrographs, electron micrographs and drawings of typical plant and animal cells.
Compare typical plant and animal cells.
State that cells use ATP from respiration for energy-requiring processes.
Outline the key structural features of a typical bacterium.
Compare a typical bacterium with typical plant and animal cells.
State that viruses are non-cellular, with a DNA or RNA core, a protein capsid and in some an outer phospholipid envelope.
Describe and carry out the Benedict's, iodine, emulsion and biuret tests.
Carry out a standardised semi-quantitative Benedict's test to estimate the concentration of a reducing sugar.
Test for non-reducing sugars using acid hydrolysis and Benedict's solution.
Describe and draw the ring forms of alpha- and beta-glucose.
Define monomer, polymer, macromolecule, monosaccharide, disaccharide and polysaccharide.
State that covalent bonds join smaller molecules into polymers.
State that glucose, fructose and maltose are reducing sugars and sucrose is not.
Describe how condensation forms glycosidic bonds in disaccharides (including sucrose) and polysaccharides.
Describe the hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds, linked to the non-reducing sugar test.
Describe the structures of starch (amylose and amylopectin) and glycogen and relate them to their functions.
Describe the structure of cellulose and how the arrangement of its molecules gives cell walls their function.
Describe triglycerides as non-polar, hydrophobic molecules made from glycerol and saturated or unsaturated fatty acids joined by ester bonds.
Relate the structure of triglycerides to their functions.
Describe phospholipids with hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty acid tails.
Describe and draw the general structure of an amino acid and the formation and breakage of a peptide bond.
Explain primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure.
Describe the interactions that hold proteins in shape: hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and covalent (including disulfide) bonds.
State that globular proteins are generally soluble with physiological roles and fibrous proteins generally insoluble with structural roles.
Describe haemoglobin as a globular protein of two alpha chains, two beta chains and haem groups.
Relate the structure of haemoglobin, including the iron in haem, to its function.
Describe collagen as a fibrous protein and how its molecules form fibres.
Relate the structure of collagen molecules and fibres to their function.
Explain hydrogen bonding between water molecules and relate solvent action, high specific heat capacity and latent heat of vaporisation to the roles of water in organisms.
State that enzymes are globular proteins acting inside cells or secreted to act outside them.
Explain enzyme action in terms of active site, enzyme-substrate complex, lower activation energy and specificity, including lock-and-key and induced fit.
Investigate the progress of enzyme reactions by product formation (catalase) and substrate disappearance (amylase).
Outline the use of a colorimeter to follow enzyme reactions that involve a colour change.
Investigate and explain the effects of temperature, pH (with buffers), enzyme, substrate and inhibitor concentration on rate.
Explain how Vmax is used to derive Km and how Km compares enzymes' affinity for their substrates.
Explain the effects of competitive and non-competitive reversible inhibitors.
Compare enzymes immobilised in alginate with free enzymes and state the advantages of immobilisation.
Describe the fluid mosaic model with reference to the hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions that form the bilayer and place the proteins.
Describe where cholesterol, glycolipids and glycoproteins lie in cell surface membranes.
Describe the roles of membrane components in stability, fluidity, permeability, transport, cell signalling and cell recognition.
Outline cell signalling: ligands secreted, transported to target cells and bound to receptors.

children.name: Movement into and out of cells

objectives.text: Describe and explain simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis.
Investigate diffusion and osmosis with plant tissue, Visking tubing and agar.
Show by calculation that surface area to volume ratio decreases as size increases.
Investigate the effect of surface area to volume ratio on diffusion with agar blocks.
Estimate the water potential of a plant tissue from immersion in solutions of different water potentials.
Explain water movement in terms of water potential and its different effects on plant and animal cells.

children.name: Replication and division of nuclei and cells

objectives.text: Describe chromosome structure: DNA, histones, sister chromatids, centromere and telomeres.
Explain the importance of mitosis in growth, replacement, repair and asexual reproduction.
Outline the mitotic cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2), mitosis and cytokinesis.
Outline how telomeres prevent loss of genes during DNA replication.
Outline the role of stem cells in cell replacement and tissue repair.
Explain how uncontrolled cell division can produce a tumour.
Describe the behaviour of chromosomes, nuclear envelope, cell membrane and spindle in prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Interpret photomicrographs, diagrams and slides of dividing cells and identify the stages of mitosis.

children.name: Structure of nucleic acids and replication of DNA

objectives.text: Describe the structure of nucleotides, including ATP (no structural formulae).
State that adenine and guanine are double-ring purines and cytosine, thymine and uracil single-ring pyrimidines.
Describe DNA as an antiparallel double helix with complementary base pairing, different hydrogen bonding in C-G and A-T and phosphodiester bonds.
Describe semi-conservative replication in S phase, with DNA polymerase, DNA ligase and leading and lagging strands.
Describe the structure of an RNA molecule, using mRNA.
State that a gene is a sequence of nucleotides in DNA that codes for a polypeptide.
Describe the universal genetic code of triplets coding for amino acids, start and stop codons.
Describe transcription and translation, with the roles of RNA polymerase, mRNA, codons, tRNA, anticodons and ribosomes.
State that the transcribed strand is the template strand and the other the non-transcribed strand.
Explain how introns are removed and exons joined to form eukaryotic mRNA.
State that a gene mutation is a change in the base sequence that may alter a polypeptide.
Explain substitution, deletion and insertion mutations and how each may affect the polypeptide.
Draw plan diagrams of transverse sections of herbaceous dicotyledonous stems, roots and leaves.
Describe the distribution of xylem and phloem in those sections.
Draw and label xylem vessel elements, sieve tube elements and companion cells.
Relate the structure of xylem vessel elements, sieve tube elements and companion cells to their functions.
State that some mineral ions and organic compounds are transported dissolved in water.
Describe water transport from soil to xylem by the apoplast and symplast pathways, with the endodermis, Casparian strip and suberin.
Explain transpiration as evaporation from internal leaf surfaces and diffusion of water vapour out.
Explain how hydrogen bonding gives cohesion-tension in the xylem and adhesion to cellulose walls.
Make annotated drawings of xerophytic leaf sections to explain how they reduce water loss.
State that assimilates move in sieve tubes from sources to sinks.
Explain how companion cells load sieve tubes using proton pumps and cotransporter proteins.
Explain mass flow in sieve tubes down a hydrostatic pressure gradient.
State that mammals have a closed double circulation of heart, blood and vessels.
Describe the functions of the pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, aorta and vena cava.
Recognise arteries, veins and capillaries and make plan diagrams of arteries and veins in TS and LS.
Relate the structures of muscular and elastic arteries, veins and capillaries to their functions.
Recognise and draw red blood cells, monocytes, neutrophils and lymphocytes.
Relate the solvent action and high specific heat capacity of water to its role in transport.
State the functions of tissue fluid and describe its formation in a capillary network.

children.name: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide

objectives.text: Describe how red blood cells transport oxygen and carbon dioxide, with haemoglobin, carbonic anhydrase, haemoglobinic acid and carbaminohaemoglobin.
Describe and explain the importance of the chloride shift.
Describe the role of plasma in carbon dioxide transport.
Describe and explain the oxygen dissociation curve of adult haemoglobin.
Explain the importance of the curve at the partial pressures of the lungs and respiring tissues.
Describe and explain the importance of the Bohr shift.
Describe the external and internal structure of the heart.
Explain the different wall thicknesses of atria and ventricles and of the left and right ventricles.
Describe the cardiac cycle, relating pressure changes in systole and diastole to the valves.
Explain the roles of the sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node and Purkyne tissue.
Describe the structure of the human gas exchange system (lungs, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, capillary network).
Describe the distribution of cartilage, ciliated epithelium, goblet cells, alveolar squamous epithelium, smooth muscle and capillaries.
Recognise those tissues in slides and micrographs.
Recognise the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli and draw plan diagrams of the trachea and bronchus wall.
Describe how ciliated epithelial cells, goblet cells and mucous glands keep the system healthy.
Describe the functions of cartilage, smooth muscle, elastic fibres and squamous epithelium.
Describe gas exchange between alveolar air and capillary blood.
State that infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and are transmissible.
Name the pathogens of cholera, malaria, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS and their type.
Explain how cholera, malaria, TB and HIV are transmitted.
Discuss the biological, social and economic factors in preventing and controlling cholera, malaria, TB and HIV.
Outline how penicillin acts on bacteria and why antibiotics do not affect viruses.
Discuss the consequences of antibiotic resistance and how to reduce its impact.
Describe how phagocytes (macrophages and neutrophils) act.
Explain what an antigen is and distinguish self from non-self antigens.
Describe the primary immune response with the roles of macrophages, B-lymphocytes and plasma cells, T-helper and T-killer cells.
Explain the role of memory cells in the secondary response and long-term immunity.
Relate the molecular structure of antibodies to their functions.
Outline the hybridoma method for producing monoclonal antibodies.
Outline the principles of using monoclonal antibodies to diagnose and treat disease.
Distinguish active from passive and natural from artificial immunity.
Explain that vaccines contain antigens that stimulate long-term immunity.
Explain how vaccination programmes help to control infectious diseases.

topics.name: A Level subject content
topics.description: Topics 12-19: A Level only; examined in Paper 4, with AS content assumed.

objectives.text: Outline the need for energy in active transport, movement and anabolic reactions such as DNA replication and protein synthesis.
Describe the features that make ATP suitable as the universal energy currency.
State that ATP is made by substrate-linked phosphorylation and by chemiosmosis in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Explain the relative energy values of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins as respiratory substrates.
State that RQ is the ratio of carbon dioxide molecules produced to oxygen molecules taken in.
Calculate RQ values of substrates from respiration equations.
Use simple respirometers to determine the RQ of germinating seeds or small invertebrates.
State the sites of glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
Outline glycolysis: phosphorylation of glucose, splitting of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into triose phosphates and oxidation to pyruvate with ATP and reduced NAD.
Explain that pyruvate enters mitochondria for the link reaction when oxygen is available.
Describe the link reaction, including the role of coenzyme A.
Outline the Krebs cycle from oxaloacetate and acetyl CoA to citrate and back.
Explain decarboxylation, dehydrogenation and the reduction of NAD and FAD in the Krebs cycle.
Describe how NAD and FAD carry hydrogen to the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Explain oxidative phosphorylation: electron transport, proton pumping, chemiosmosis through ATP synthase and oxygen as final electron acceptor.
Relate the structure of mitochondria to their function.
Outline lactate fermentation in mammals and ethanol fermentation in yeast.
Explain why aerobic respiration yields much more energy than anaerobic respiration.
Explain how rice is adapted to grow with submerged roots.
Use redox indicators (DCPIP, methylene blue) to investigate the effects of temperature and substrate concentration on yeast respiration.
Use simple respirometers to investigate the effect of temperature on respiration rate.

children.name: Photosynthesis as an energy transfer process

objectives.text: Relate chloroplast structure, from diagrams and electron micrographs, to function.
Explain that ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage drive the Calvin cycle.
State that thylakoids are the site of the light-dependent stage and the stroma of the light-independent stage.
Describe the roles of chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotene and xanthophyll in light absorption.
Interpret absorption and action spectra.
Use chromatography and Rf values to separate and identify chloroplast pigments.
State that cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation occur in the light-dependent stage.
Explain cyclic photophosphorylation (PSI only, photoactivation, ATP).
Explain non-cyclic photophosphorylation (PSI and PSII, photolysis of water, ATP and reduced NADP).
Explain electron transport, proton pumping and chemiosmosis across the thylakoid membrane.
Outline the three stages of the Calvin cycle: fixation by rubisco, reduction of GP to TP, regeneration of RuBP.
State that GP is used for some amino acids and TP for carbohydrates, lipids and amino acids.
State that light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature are limiting factors.
Explain how these factors affect the rate of photosynthesis.
Use redox indicators and chloroplast suspensions to investigate light intensity and wavelength.
Use whole plants, including aquatic plants, to investigate light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.
Explain what homeostasis is and why it matters in mammals.
Explain homeostasis in terms of stimuli, receptors, nervous and endocrine coordination, effectors and negative feedback.
State that urea is made in the liver by deamination of excess amino acids.
Describe the structure of the kidney.
Identify the parts of a nephron and its blood vessels.
Describe and explain ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule and selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Relate the structure of the Bowman's capsule and proximal convoluted tubule to their functions.
Describe the roles of the hypothalamus, posterior pituitary, ADH, aquaporins and collecting ducts in osmoregulation.
Describe cell signalling by glucagon: receptor, G-protein, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A and the amplifying enzyme cascade.
Explain negative feedback control of blood glucose by insulin (muscle and liver) and glucagon (liver).
Explain how test strips and biosensors measure glucose, with glucose oxidase and peroxidase.
Explain how stomatal opening and closing balances carbon dioxide uptake against water loss.
Explain that stomata have daily rhythms of opening and closing.
Describe guard cells and explain how they open and close stomata.
Describe the role of abscisic acid and calcium ions in closing stomata under water stress.
Describe the endocrine system with reference to ADH, glucagon and insulin.
Compare the nervous and endocrine systems.
Describe sensory and motor neurones and state that intermediate neurones connect them.
Outline how sensory receptor cells detect stimuli and start impulses.
Describe how an action potential arises in a sensory neurone, using a taste-bud chemoreceptor.
Describe and explain the resting potential, the action potential and the restoration of the resting potential.
Describe and explain saltatory conduction in myelinated neurones.
Explain how the refractory period limits the frequency of impulses.
Describe the structure and function of a cholinergic synapse, including calcium ions.
Describe the roles of neuromuscular junctions, T-tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum in stimulating contraction.
Describe the ultrastructure of striated muscle and the sarcomere.
Explain the sliding filament model with troponin, tropomyosin, calcium ions and ATP.
Describe and explain the rapid closure of the Venus fly trap.
Explain how auxin causes elongation growth by stimulating proton pumping that acidifies cell walls.
Describe the role of gibberellin in the germination of barley.

children.name: Passage of information from parents to offspring

objectives.text: Explain the terms haploid (n) and diploid (2n).
Explain homologous pairs of chromosomes.
Explain why gamete production needs a reduction division.
Describe chromosome behaviour and the nuclear envelope, membrane and spindle in the stages of meiosis I and II.
Interpret photomicrographs and diagrams of meiosis and identify its stages.
Explain how crossing over and random orientation in meiosis produce genetically different gametes.
Explain how random fusion of gametes produces genetically different individuals.

children.name: The roles of genes in determining the phenotype

objectives.text: Explain gene, locus, allele, dominant, recessive, codominant, linkage, test cross, F1, F2, phenotype, genotype, homozygous and heterozygous.
Use genetic diagrams and Punnett squares for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses with dominance, codominance, multiple alleles and sex linkage.
Use genetic diagrams for dihybrid crosses with autosomal linkage and epistasis.
Use genetic diagrams to explain and predict test crosses.
Use the chi-squared test (formula provided) to test the significance of differences between observed and expected results.
Explain how genes, proteins and phenotype are related for TYR (albinism), HBB (sickle cell anaemia), F8 (haemophilia) and HTT (Huntington's disease).
Explain how the Le and le alleles affect gibberellin synthesis and stem elongation.
Distinguish structural from regulatory genes and repressible from inducible enzymes.
Explain the control of protein production in a prokaryote using the lac operon.
State that transcription factors bind DNA and raise or lower transcription in eukaryotes.
Explain how gibberellin activates genes by causing breakdown of DELLA repressor proteins.
Explain, with examples, that variation has genetic, environmental or combined causes.
Explain discontinuous and continuous variation.
Explain the genetic basis of discontinuous and continuous variation.
Use the t-test (formula provided) to compare the means of two samples.
Explain natural selection in terms of overproduction, competition, survival of the best adapted and inheritance of their alleles.
Explain stabilising, disruptive and directional selection.
Explain how selection, the founder effect, genetic drift and the bottleneck effect change allele frequencies.
Outline antibiotic resistance in bacteria as an example of natural selection.
Use the Hardy-Weinberg principle (equations provided) and state when it applies.
Describe the principles of selective breeding.
Outline selective breeding for disease resistance in wheat and rice, hybrid maize, and milk yield in dairy cattle.
Outline evolution as the formation of new species through changes in gene pools over generations.
Discuss how DNA sequence data show evolutionary relationships.
Explain allopatric and sympatric speciation through genetic isolation.
Discuss the biological, morphological and ecological species concepts.
Describe the three domains Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
State that Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes differing in membrane lipids, ribosomal RNA and cell walls.
Describe the taxonomic hierarchy within Eukarya.
Outline the features of the kingdoms Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Outline how viruses are classified by nucleic acid type and strandedness.
Define ecosystem and niche.
Explain that biodiversity is assessed at the levels of ecosystems and habitats, species and their abundance, and genetic variation.
Explain why random sampling matters in assessing biodiversity.
Use quadrats, line and belt transects and mark-release-recapture with the Lincoln index (formula provided).
Use Spearman's rank and Pearson's linear correlation (formulae provided) to analyse relationships, including biotic and abiotic effects on distribution.
Use Simpson's index of diversity (formula provided) and interpret its values.
Explain how climate change, competition, hunting and habitat loss can cause extinction.
Outline reasons for maintaining biodiversity.
Outline the roles of zoos, botanic gardens, conserved areas, frozen zoos and seed banks.
Describe IVF, embryo transfer and surrogacy in conserving endangered mammals.
Explain reasons for controlling invasive alien species.
Outline the roles of IUCN and CITES in conservation.
Define recombinant DNA.
Explain genetic engineering as deliberate manipulation of genetic material, which may involve transferring a gene so it is expressed.
Explain that genes for transfer may be extracted, made from mRNA or synthesised from nucleotides.
Explain the roles of restriction endonucleases, DNA ligase, plasmids, DNA polymerase and reverse transcriptase.
Explain why a promoter may be transferred with the gene.
Explain how marker genes for fluorescent products confirm gene expression.
Explain gene editing as insertion, deletion or replacement of DNA at specific sites.
Describe and explain PCR, including the role of Taq polymerase.
Describe and explain gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments.
Outline how microarrays are used to analyse genomes and detect mRNA.
Outline the benefits of sequence and protein-structure databases.
Explain the advantages of recombinant human proteins: insulin, factor VIII and adenosine deaminase.
Outline the advantages of genetic screening for BRCA1 and BRCA2, Huntington's disease and cystic fibrosis.
Outline gene therapy for SCID and inherited eye diseases.
Discuss the social and ethical considerations of genetic screening and gene therapy.
Explain how GM salmon, herbicide-resistant soybean and insect-resistant cotton may help to meet the demand for food.
Discuss the ethical and social implications of GMOs in food production.

topics.name: Practical skills
topics.description: Not a content section of the syllabus: our grouping of the practical assessment section (Papers 3 and 5) and the Mathematical requirements.

children.name: Advanced practical skills (Paper 3)
children.description: AS Level: manipulation, measurement and observation; presentation of data and observations; analysis, conclusions and evaluation, including light microscopy.

objectives.text: Decide on variables, ranges, intervals, replicates, controls and standardised variables in an investigation.
Collect data safely, assessing risk, and record raw and processed results in well-headed tables to an appropriate precision.
Display data as graphs, bar charts or histograms drawn to the stated conventions.
Interpret data, identify anomalies, draw conclusions and identify errors and improvements.
Set up a light microscope, make a stained temporary slide and find and draw specified tissues and cells.
Draw plan diagrams and cell drawings to the stated conventions and record observable similarities and differences.
Measure and calculate actual sizes using magnifications, scale bars, graticules and stage micrometers, and estimate numbers of cells in an area.

children.name: Planning, analysis and evaluation (Paper 5)
children.description: A Level: planning, analysis, conclusions and evaluation, with the A Level statistics of the Mathematical requirements.

objectives.text: State a prediction linked to a hypothesis and identify the variables to change, measure and standardise.
Describe a method with suitable concentrations (serial or proportional dilution), controls, replicates and a risk assessment.
Process given data, choose and justify a statistical test, state a null hypothesis and draw conclusions.
Evaluate anomalies, replication, ranges, measurement methods and control of variables, and judge validity and confidence.
Use mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation, standard error and 95% confidence intervals (formulae provided).
Plot error bars and judge whether differences between means are likely to be significant.
Distinguish normal from non-normal distributions and correlation from causation.
